title: Temporary Tables, Table Variables, and Variables
description: Store intermediate results with temporary tables and table variables. Use stored procedure variables and OUTPUT parameters for flexible T-SQL programs.

data.text: Sometimes you need to hold intermediate results within a query or procedure. Temporary tables and table variables are the two main ways to do this in SQL Server. Each has its own strengths: temp tables for large data sets, table variables for small ones.

A temporary table (#table) is a real table that exists only for the duration of a session or procedure. Local temp tables (single #) are visible only to the creating session; global temp tables (##) are visible to all sessions.

data.title: Creating and using a local temp table
data.code:
-- # means local temp table
CREATE TABLE #top_products (
    product_id   INT,
    product_name NVARCHAR(100),
    sales        MONEY
);

INSERT INTO #top_products
SELECT TOP 5 p.product_id, p.product_name, SUM(i.quantity * i.list_price) AS sales
FROM   production.products p
INNER JOIN sales.order_items i ON i.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
ORDER BY sales DESC;

rows: Dropped when last referencing proc ends

data.title: Temp tables in tempdb
data.text: Temporary tables are created in tempdb, not your database. This means they are fast (memory-optimized in modern SQL Server) and automatically cleaned up. They also benefit from automatic statistics, unlike table variables.

A table variable (@variable) is declared with DECLARE and has a more limited scope — it exists only within the current batch. Table variables do not maintain statistics and are best for small result sets (under ~1,000 rows).

data.title: Declaring and using a table variable
Table variable vs. temp table
data.text: Table variables: less locking, no statistics, good for small sets. Temp tables: real statistics, better for large sets and complex joins. When in doubt, test both and check the execution plan.

data.text: OUTPUT parameters let a stored procedure return scalar values to the caller — useful for calculated counts, totals, or status codes that you want back in T-SQL variables.
